books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: Spain moved sugar production to Europe, where free labor was plentiful.
options.misconception: Sugarcane needs a hot climate; it could not move to Europe.

options.text: Spain freed all enslaved workers in the colonies and paid wages to everyone.
options.misconception: Spain expanded slavery in this period; it did not free workers or pay wages.

options.text: Spain ended sugar production in the Americas and switched to growing wheat instead.
options.misconception: Sugar only grew; the labor crisis was solved by bringing in workers, not by ending sugar.

options.text: Spain turned to enslaved African labor, first used on the Atlantic island plantations.

rationales.general:
1. Start with the crop. Sugar needed many workers at every stage, as the engraving shows.
2. Ask what happened to the workers. Disease emptied Native towns, so the labor supply collapsed.
3. Find the recipe that already existed. Madeira and São Tomé ran sugar plantations on enslaved African labor.
4. Rule out the rest. Spain did not end sugar, free workers, or move cane to Europe.
Remember: when a labor-hungry crop loses its workers, ask where the same crop already had workers.
rationales.D: Disease emptied the Native towns, so Spain turned to enslaved African labor, already used on the Atlantic island plantations.
rationales.A: Sugarcane needs a hot climate. It could not move to Europe.
rationales.B: Spain expanded slavery in this period. It did not free workers or pay wages.
rationales.C: Sugar only grew. The labor crisis was solved by bringing in workers, not by ending sugar.

stem: Sugar was the hungriest crop of all for labor. As Native towns emptied from disease, what did the labor system shown in the engraving lead Spain to do?

stimulus.source_note: Jan Collaert I after Jan van der Straet (Stradanus), 'The Invention of Sugar Refinery', Nova Reperta plate 13, c. 1600, Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain (CC0).
stimulus.text: The engraving shows a sugar refinery in the Americas around 1600. In the background, workers cut sugarcane in the fields. Inside, workers crush the cane, boil the juice in large vats over fires, and pour the syrup into cone-shaped molds to form sugar loaves. The work is done by hand, in stages, by many workers at once.
